20 An extension–force graph for a spring is shown.
15
extension / cm
0
0
6.0
force / N
What is the spring constant of the spring?
A
0.025 N m–1
B
0.40 N m–1
C
2.5 N m–1
D
40 N m–1

hints: Notice the axes are swapped from the usual $F$-$x$ plot: extension in cm is vertical up to 15 and force in N is horizontal up to 6.0.
Recall Hooke's law $F = kx$, so $k = F/x$; on this extension-force plot $k$ is 1 divided by the gradient, not the gradient itself.
Convert the 15 cm extension to $0.15 \text{ m}$ before dividing the 6.0 N force by it to obtain $k$ in $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Read the end point of the straight line through the origin: force $F = 6.0 \text{ N}$ produces extension $x = 15 \text{ cm}$.
State Hooke's law for the spring: $F = kx$, so the spring constant is $k = F/x$.
Convert extension to SI units for $k$ in $\text{N m}^{-1}$: $x = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$.
Substitute: $k = 6.0/0.15 = 40$ $\text{N m}^{-1}$, checking units are force divided by length. This is option D.

A.explanation: This is $x/F$ in SI units, $0.15/6.0 = 0.025$, which inverts Hooke's law $F = kx$.

B.explanation: This is $6.0/15 = 0.40$ using extension in cm, leaving the answer in $\text{N cm}^{-1}$ instead of $\text{N m}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: This is $15/6.0 = 2.5$, which is extension divided by force with no cm to m conversion.

D.explanation: This is $k = F/x = 6.0/0.15 = 40$ $\text{N m}^{-1}$ after converting extension to metres.
